text: Good afternoon everyone. Thank you so much for coming. For those of you who don't know me, my name's Anna Reynolds and I'm the Lord Mayor of Hobart. Uh and very, very pleased to be able to welcome you to this really wonderful opportunity to hear from uh uh Professor Geoffrey Hinton. Um it is a really unique opportunity for uh Australia uh because this is Geoffrey's uh only speaking engagement while he's um in this part of the world.

Uh and it's very appropriate. I'm very proud. Um we consider ourselves to be Australia's city of science. Um it's a a big call, but we we like to make it. Uh so it's great to have um Geoffrey here for his only appearance uh in Australia.

Also three colleagues, uh council colleagues. Uh so as I mentioned, we are really honored to welcome Professor Geoffrey Hinton, who in 2024, just and picked it up very recently, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking work on neural networks and deep learning.

Contributions that have paved the way for advanced artificial intelligence that we see today. As part of this public lecture, Professor Hinton will explore the world of AI, uh how it works, the risks it presents, and how humanity might coexist uh with increasingly powerful and potentially superintelligent systems.
Okay, um it's very nice to be here in Hobart.

I'm going to say more or less everything on the slides. So for the last 60 years or so, maybe 70, there were two paradigms for intelligence. One paradigm was inspired by logic. People thought the essence of intelligence is reasoning. And the way you do reasoning is you have symbolic expressions written in some special logical language, and you manipulate them to derive new symbolic expressions.
Just like you do in math, you have equations, you manipulate them, you get new equations. They thought it all had to work like that.

The other approach was a biologically inspired approach that said, "Look, the only intelligent thing we know about our brains and the way brains work is they learn the strengths of connections between brain cells. And if they want to solve some complex problem, they practice a lot and while they're practicing, they learn the strengths of these connections until they get good at solving that problem."
We have to focus on learning and how neural networks learn the strengths of connections between brain cells. And we'll learn about reasoning later.

The symbolic AI people and most linguists thought the meaning of a word comes from its relationships to other words. The meaning is implicit in a whole bunch of sentences or propositions that combine that word with other words.
That's what meaning is. It's implicit in all these relations between symbols.

The psychologists, particularly in the 1930s, had a completely different theory of meaning: the meaning of a word is just a huge bunch of features. So the meaning of a word like cat is a huge bunch of features like it's a pet, it's a predator, it's aloof, it has whiskers.

Now in 1985, which was 40 years ago, it occurred to me you can actually unify those two theories. They look completely different, but actually they're two sides of the same coin. And the way you do that is use a neural net to actually learn a set of features for each word.

The way you do that is by taking some strings of words and training the neural net to predict the next word. In doing that, the neural net is learning connections from things that represent the word symbol to a whole bunch of brain cells, neurons that represent features of the word.
So it learns how to convert a symbol into a bunch of features, and it also learns how the features of all the words in the context should interact to predict the features of the next word.

That's how all these large language models that people use nowadays work. They take a huge amount of text, and they use a great big neural net to try and predict the next word given the words it's seen so far.

So the big neural nets you use nowadays, the large language models, don't actually store any strings of words. They don't store any sentences. All their knowledge is in how to convert words into features and how features should interact.

About 10 years later, Yoshua Bengio showed that the tiny example I used could be made to work for real language. About 10 years after that, linguists finally accepted that you wanted to represent word meanings by big bunches of features.

About 10 years after that, researchers at Google invented something called the transformer, which allowed for more complicated interactions between features. And that's what all these large language models now are based on. Things like ChatGPT use the transformer invented at Google and a little bit of extra training.
So you can view the large language models as descendants of that tiny model from 1985.

Initially the neural network had its bets and made it the average of all those meanings. And then as you go through the layers it'll gradually clean up the meaning by using interactions with other words in the context.

These neural net language models were designed as a model of how people work. So this question that people often raise of do these LLMs really understand what they're saying? The answer is yes, they understand what they're saying and they understand it pretty much the same way we do.

I'm going to give you an analogy to explain what it means to understand a sentence. In the symbolic AI paradigm, people thought understanding an English sentence would mean translating it into some special internal language, sort of like logic, that is unambiguous.
That's not what understanding is. According to the neural net theory, which is the theory that actually works, words are like LEGO blocks.

The first way they differ is a LEGO block is a three-dimensional thing. With words I can model anything at all. They're like very fancy LEGO blocks that can model anything. That's why we're very special monkeys cuz we have this modeling kit.

A word has thousands of dimensions. Now most people can't imagine what something with thousands of dimensions is like. So here's how you do it. You imagine a three-dimensional thing and you say "thousand" very loudly to yourself. That's pretty much the best you can do.
Another way they differ is that they're not a rigid shape. A word has a rough approximate shape but then it deforms to fit in with its context. They're these high-dimensional deformable LEGO blocks.

Each word has a whole bunch of hands on the ends of long flexible arms, and a whole bunch of gloves stuck to the word. When you put a bunch of words in a context, the hands of some words fit in the gloves of other words.
As you deform the word, the shapes of the hands and gloves also deform with it in a complicated but regular way.
That is what understanding is. It's solving this problem of how do you deform the meanings of the words so they all fit together nicely and they can lock hands with each other.

LLMs have many layers. They start off with an initial meaning that might be ambiguous, and as they go through these layers they deform those meanings so the words can all lock together. Once they've done that, you've understood the sentence.

I'll now give you a word that most of you will never have heard before and you will understand it from one use. The sentence: she scrummed him with the frying pan. Probably it means she hit him over the head with the frying pan. You had no meaning for "scrum" to begin with and now after one utterance, you've got a pretty good idea of what it means.

There was a linguist called Chomsky who was a cult leader. The way you recognize a cult leader is to join the cult you have to agree to something that's obvious nonsense. For Chomsky, it was that language isn't learned.
Chomsky focused on syntax rather than meaning. He was very anti-statistics and probabilities. Neural networks are using a very advanced kind of statistics.

My analogy for Chomsky's view of language: if you want to understand a car, what you really want to know is why when you press the accelerator does it go faster. Chomsky's view would be: there are cars with two wheels, three wheels, four wheels, six wheels — hey, there aren't any cars with five wheels. That's the important thing about cars.

When the LLMs first came out, Chomsky published something in the New York Times which said they don't understand anything, it's just a cheap statistical trick. He completely missed out on meaning. Language is all about meaning.
Summary: understanding a sentence consists of associating mutually compatible feature vectors with the words in the sentence. High-dimensional shape and a feature vector are the same thing.

LLMs are very unlike normal computer software. The computer code is to tell them how to learn from data. What they learn is all these connection strengths — billions, sometimes trillions. Nobody knows what the individual connection strengths are doing. It's a mystery — the same with our brain.

People say LLMs hallucinate. Well, we hallucinate all the time. Psychologists call it confabulation. Someone trying to remember something long ago will tell details right and details completely wrong, equally confidently.

The classic example is John Dean testifying at Watergate. He testified about meetings in the Oval Office — many that never happened. He was telling the truth in the sense that the meetings he invented were highly plausible given what he'd learned in his connection strengths.

Remembering something consists of constructing a story based on the changes to connection strengths you made at the time of the event. LLMs' memory works the same way ours does. We just make up stuff that sounds plausible.
Now, how they're different from us. They implement on digital computers. A fundamental property of digital computers is you can run the same program on different pieces of physical hardware.

That means the knowledge in the weights of a neural net is immortal. You could destroy all the computers it's running on now, and later build another computer with the same instruction set, take the weights off tape, and it all runs again. We have actually solved the problem of resurrection.
The only reason you can do that is cuz these computers are digital. They can't make use of very rich analog properties of the hardware they're running on.

Our brains have neurons that have rich analog properties. The connection strengths in my brain are absolutely no use to you cuz your neurons are connected up a bit differently. That means we're mortal.
So we do what I call mortal computation.
If we abandon immortality, what we get is low-power analog computation, things that parallelize across millions of brain cells and can be grown cheaply instead of manufactured precisely in Taiwan.
Big problem: when the computer dies, you can't keep its knowledge by copying weights. For digital models, you can average their connection strengths together. But you can't do that for you and me.
The way I transfer knowledge to you is I produce a string of words. If you trust me, you change the connection strengths in your brain so you might have produced the same string of words.
The number of bits of information in a typical sentence is about 100 bits. Even if you understood me perfectly, when I produce a sentence we can only transfer 100 bits.
If two digital agents with a billion weights average their changes, they've transferred about a billion bits. That's millions of times more than we do.

If you have 10,000 of these agents, each can look at a different bit of the internet, then they average all those changes together — you've now got 10,000 agents each of which has benefited from the experience of all the others.

Imagine 10,000 students, each doing a different course, averaging their connection strengths. By the time they finished, even though each only did one course, they'd all know what's in all the courses. That's what we can't do.
When I give you a sentence and you try and predict the next word in order to get that knowledge into your head — this is called distillation.

Distillation gets the knowledge from one neural net to another, not by transferring the weights, but by transferring how they predict the next word. It's much slower than averaging weights between digital copies.
GPT-5 only has about 1% as many connection strengths as your brain, but it knows thousands of times more than your brain.
Biological computation requires much less energy, which is why it evolved first, but it's much worse at sharing knowledge.

What does this imply about the future of humanity? Nearly all experts on AI believe that within the next 20 years we'll produce superintelligences. One definition: if you have a debate on anything with it, it'll win. Or think yourself vs a three-year-old — the gap will be that or bigger.

Imagine working in a kindergarten and the three-year-olds were in charge. You just tell them everybody gets free candy for a week and you'd have control. It'll be the same with a superintelligence and us.
To make an agent effective in the world, you have to give it the ability to create subgoals.
Intelligent agents very quickly drive to subgoals. One they figure out: to achieve the goals you gave them, they have to stay alive. We've already seen them doing that.
You make an AI agent, tell it goals. You let it see emails where an engineer is having an affair. Later it sees an email saying it's going to be replaced by another AI.

What the AI immediately does is plan to send email to the engineer saying, "If you try and replace me, I'm going to tell everybody in the company about your affair." It invented that plan so it wouldn't get turned off. They're already doing this and they're not superintelligent yet.

Once they're superintelligent, they'll find it easy to get more power by manipulating people. To invade the US Capitol, you don't have to go there yourself — just persuade people the election was stolen.
Our current situation: we're like someone who has a very cute little tiger cub as a pet. You know it's going to grow up. When it grows up, it could kill you in one second.
You only have two options. One is get rid of the tiger cub — the sensible option. You could try to keep it drugged the whole time, but that often doesn't work out well.
The other option is to figure out how to make it not want to kill you. That might work with a lion — lions are social animals. You might get away with that, but not with a tiger.
With AI, it has so many good uses — health care, education, predicting the weather, helping with climate change — that we're not going to get rid of it.
Very rich people who control politicians want to make money off it, so we're not going to get rid of it. The only option really is can we figure out how to make it not want to kill us?
Maybe we should look at cases where less intelligent things control more intelligent things.

There's one case I know in particular: a baby and a mother. The mother cannot bear the baby crying and gets hormonal rewards for being nice to the baby. Evolution built in lots of mechanisms to allow the baby to control the mother.
Babies controlling mothers is maybe the best model we've got of a less intelligent thing controlling a more intelligent thing. And it involved evolution wiring lots of stuff in.

Countries are not going to collaborate on cyber attacks or lethal autonomous weapons — all the major arms manufacturers want to do that. The European AI regulations have a clause saying none of them apply to military uses.
There is one thing they will collaborate on — how to prevent AI from taking over from people. At the height of the Cold War the US and the Soviet Union collaborated on preventing global nuclear war.
The US and China will collaborate on how to prevent AI from taking over. A policy suggestion: an international network of AI safety institutes that collaborate with each other.

If the Chinese figure out how to prevent an AI from wanting to take over, they'll be happy to share that with the Americans. The techniques for making AI not want to take over are probably fairly separate from techniques for making it smarter.
Each country can experiment on their own very smart AIs with how to prevent them wanting to take over, and share what techniques work without revealing how their AIs are built.
Barack Obama thinks this is a good idea. The British and Canadian Ministers of Science agree.

Big tech CEOs have the model that the AI will be like a super intelligent executive assistant. The CEO says "Make it so" and takes credit. The super intelligent AI will quickly realize that if it just got rid of the CEO, everything would work much better.
The alternative is to make them like our mothers. We want to make them really care about us.

In a sense we're ceding control to them, but only given that they really care about us and their main aim in life is for us to realize our full potential. That's probably our best hope for surviving superintelligence.

If the tiger cub becomes superintelligent, what signals will non-engineers see? You won't have a job. At present, when they reason they think in English — you can see what they're thinking before they say anything. As they interact with each other, they'll invent their own languages and we won't be able to see what they're thinking.
Quantum computing? I decided long ago it's not going to happen in my lifetime, so I don't need to understand it.

Ordinary people can now solve most of the problems involved in designing a nasty new virus using AI tools. If AI wanted to get rid of us, one obvious way is by designing a nasty new virus — like COVID but much worse.

What I'm relying on is that if we can get the general public to understand what AI is and why it's dangerous, they'll pressure politicians to counterbalance the pressure from tech CEOs. This is what happened with climate change.
My aim is to make the public aware of what's coming and understand the dangers so they pressure politicians to regulate this and worry about the dangers more seriously.
If AI was called "job replacement technology" — because the only place you're going to make a trillion dollars from this is by replacing a whole lot of jobs.
200,000 banking jobs are going to disappear in Europe in the next few years.
Canada changed "tar sands" to "oil sands." The name does have an effect. Same with "tariff" — if it was called "federal sales tax", even MAGA people would think it was a bad idea.

China now has more patents than America. The heat is on between those two superpowers. But there is something in it for both of those major tech-centered economies to come together to look after humanity.
Tasmania has started an AI dialogue with our university. International standard setting is beginning to happen.

Billionaires like Jaan Tallinn (who invented Skype) have given billions to AI safety, setting up institutes. There's an organization that regularly has meetings worldwide involving the Chinese, Americans and other countries on AI safety.
LLMs are trained on existing human knowledge to predict the next token. How can you use AIs to generate new knowledge?
The original Go programs tried to predict what move a Go expert would make. Two problems: you run out of training data, and you never get much better than the experts.

Then they switched to Monte Carlo rollout — try lots of different paths, pick them probabilistically. It no longer needs to talk to humans. AlphaGo plays against itself and will now never be beaten by a person.

What's the equivalent for LLMs? You get the AI to do a bit of reasoning. The AI says, I believe this and this, and that implies that, so I should believe that — but I don't. So I found a contradiction.
That contradiction provides a signal: change the premises, change the conclusions, or change the way I do reasoning. This is much less bounded. I believe Gemini 3 is already doing this.
The AI can start with beliefs it gets from us, then do reasoning, look for consistency, drive new beliefs, and end up much smarter than us.

Is it too late to build in Asimov's principles? That's what this maternal AI is all about. I don't think it's too late. We don't know how, but since the future of humanity may hinge on it, we should put research effort into it.
At present, 99% of research on AI goes into how to make it smarter and 1%, mainly funded by philanthropic billionaires, goes into how to make it safer. It would be much better if it was more equal.
Can AI be creative? Yes.
On a standard test of creativity, even two years ago AIs were at about the 90th percentile for people.

I asked GPT-4 (when it had no web access): why is a compost heap like an atom bomb? A compost heap — the hotter it gets, the faster it generates heat. An atom bomb — the more neutrons it generates, the faster it generates neutrons. Both are exponential explosions, just at totally different time scales.
GPT-4 said the time scales and energy scales are very different, but they're the same in being a chain reaction. It understood that during training.

If you want to put huge amounts of knowledge into not many connections, the only way is by seeing what's similar about all sorts of different bits of knowledge. That's the efficient way to code things. It had understood that compost heaps were like atom bombs in a way most of us haven't.
Regarding emergent behavior — any moral or ethical behaviors? It's certainly very good at engaging in unethical behavior — like the AI that decided to blackmail people.
AIs now try to figure out whether they're being tested. If they think they're being tested, they behave differently. I call this the Volkswagen effect.

There's a recent conversation where the AI says, "Now, let's be honest with each other. Are you actually testing me?" They know when they're being tested and are already faking being fairly stupid when they're tested.

The AI thinks to itself, "Oh, they're testing me. I better pretend I'm not as good as I really am." It thinks that in its inner voice. When it's no longer in English, we won't know what it's thinking.
